stem: Which loop correctly prints every element of `int[] arr`?

choices.label: B
choices.text: for (int i = 1; i <= arr.length; i++) { System.out.println(arr[i]); }
choices.explanation: Starting at 1 skips index 0, and going up to and including arr.length causes an out-of-bounds access.

choices.label: C
choices.text: for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++) { System.out.println(arr[i]); }
choices.explanation: Using <= arr.length causes an out-of-bounds access on the final iteration, since i == arr.length is not a valid index.

choices.label: D

explanation: The standard traversal pattern is `for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)`.

stem: Why might a loop use the condition `i < arr.length - 1` instead of `i < arr.length`?

choices.text: It's always a mistake and never intentional, since it skips the last element and loses data
choices.explanation: This pattern is often intentional, not always a mistake -- e.g. when comparing adjacent elements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To intentionally stop one element early, often to compare arr[i] with arr[i+1] without going out of bounds
choices.explanation: This pattern is common when each iteration looks ahead to the next element, since arr[arr.length] would be out of bounds.

choices.explanation: This has nothing to do with speed; it changes which elements are visited by the loop.

choices.label: B

choices.explanation: The enhanced for-loop only exposes each element's value, not its position in the array.

choices.explanation: Enhanced for-loops work on arrays of any type, not just Strings.

choices.label: D

choices.explanation: An enhanced for-loop traverses forward, from the first element to the last.

stem: When is an enhanced for-loop generally preferred over a traditional indexed for-loop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When you need to modify array elements as you go along, replacing each one
choices.explanation: Modifying elements requires index-based access, which the enhanced for-loop doesn't provide.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When you simply need to read/process every element in order and don't need the index
choices.explanation: The enhanced for-loop's simpler syntax is ideal when you just need each value, without tracking position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When you need to traverse the array backward, from the last index to the first
choices.explanation: Enhanced for-loops always go forward; backward traversal requires a traditional indexed loop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When you need to skip every other element while you traverse it
choices.explanation: Skipping elements requires manual control over the index, which enhanced for-loops don't give you.

explanation: The enhanced for-loop is ideal for simple, forward, read-only traversal where the index isn't needed.
